newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-BRAZIL AND ENGLAND LEARN VALUABLE LESSONS FROM TOURNOI.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BRAZIL AND ENGLAND LEARN VALUABLE LESSONS FROM TOURNOI.

text.p: Two clear points emerged from Brazil's 1-0 win over England in the Tournoi de France on Tuesday at the Parc des Princes.

The first confirmed that despite a friendly defeat to Norway and draws against France and Italy in their previous Tournoi matches, Brazil cannot be under-estimated and definitely have the potential to retain the World Cup next year.

The second is that England, despite looking tired after wins over South Africa, Poland, Italy and France in the last two weeks, are developing into a side that could make a huge impact in the finals -- providing they qualify as expected.
Young players like Sol Campbell, brothers Gary and Phil Neville and Paul Scholes were not overawed by the Brazilians, but instead learnt valuable lessons against some of the world's best players.

In fact Ronaldo, who is just about to supersede England skipper Alan Shearer as the world's most expensive player when he completes his move from Barcelona to Inter-Milan, can rarely have had a harder task against any defender. Cambpell blocked him at almost every twist and turn, and Ronaldo did not have a shot worthy of the name all match.

Despite that. a Brazilian victory was always likely against an England team lacking the snap and verve of recent weeks, but the fact Brazil only scored once also shows that England defended solidly and emphasised yet again the huge advances they have made under coach Glenn Hoddle in the last year.

The strengths of the Brazilians are well documented -- the brilliance of Ronaldo, the intelligence, pace and delivery of Romario, the shooting of Roberto Carlos. But the window has been opened for Europeans to see some impressive, less familiar names -- Djalminha, Denilson and Flavio Conceicao.

Brazilian coach Mario Zagallo, like Hoddle, said his side had learnt a number of valuable lessons from the four-team tournament, which was due to end on Wednesday night with hosts France playing Italy in Paris.
"It was very important for us to take part in this tournament against three teams preparing for the World Cup next year," he said.

"We head home now for the Copa America, but I felt we learnt a lot about ourselves playing against European teams -- more probably than we will by playing South American teams over the next few weeks.
"If we want to win the World Cup again next year we cannot relax for a minute."

Since taking over from Terry Venables after Euro 96 Hoddle's England have played 11 matches and won nine of them - - the only defeats coming against Brazil and Italy, the two finalists in the last World Cup.

England beat Italy 2-0 in Nantes last week and another victory -- albeit a far tougher one to achieve -- against the Italians in Rome will guarantee England an automatic place in the finals. Even if they lose that match they should still qualify as the best European runners-up -- and Hoddle believes his team have learnt hugely from the Tournoi which they actually ended up winning with a match to go.

"People said it was madness to play in this tournament and I think we proved our point that it was absolutely the right thing to do. We have learnt as a team and improved in all areas of the field. I am particularly happy with our overall performances.
"We lost to Brazil because so many of the players were tired, but that's not an excuse. At the same time we learnt a lot from the game and I am delighted with the way we have played here."

The only goal of an entertaining match came after 61 minutes when Romario latched on to a superbly-angled and weighted through ball from Leonardo and scored with a shot that went off David Seaman's far post.
